planting.note: Plant grafted, dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring into deep, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from juglone-sensitive garden plants; scout for husk/walnut maggot since this selection is notably susceptible.

directions: Stabler traces back to a native tree discovered around 1875 by the grandfather of Henry Stabler in the Sandy Spring area of Montgomery County, Maryland. Henry Stabler publicized the tree decades later, Dr. Robert T. Morris gave it its name, and nurseryman T.P. Littlepage introduced grafted trees commercially around 1915; it has remained in circulation for over a century chiefly because of how its medium, broadly oval nuts crack. A meaningful share of nuts come apart as a single unbroken kernel lobe rather than splitting into two halves, a trait sheller operations and hand crackers both prize, and kernel content runs around 31 percent of total nut weight. The tree is more prone to husk maggot damage than many newer named selections, so plan on monitoring and management where that pest is active. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible black walnut cultivar nearby for pollination, and keep juglone-sensitive plants like tomatoes and apples well outside the eventual dripline.
sources: Northern Nut Growers Association (1913 and 1916 Annual Report proceedings)

common_name: Hickman Black Walnut (UMCA Patented Spur-Bearing Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or manage crop load in heavy years, since this cultivar can lean toward alternate bearing without care.

directions: Hickman was selected from a controlled 2002 cross of 'Sparks 127' and 'Football' made at the University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry's New Franklin, Missouri test planting, and was granted U.S. Plant Patent PP36,382 in January 2025 as the program's first distinct cultivar released specifically for orchard kernel production. Its defining trait is a spur-bearing habit, meaning nuts cluster on short compact side branches much the way apples bear on spurs, rather than spreading thinly along long shoots, and this is linked to unusually early bearing, with flowering already recorded by the tree's fifth growing season. Kernels average roughly 5.1 grams and can reach up to 36 percent of nut weight in favorable years, well above the 10-14 percent typical of wild seedling trees, though yields can run alternate-bearing under low-input management. Site it in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with another black walnut cultivar nearby for pollination, and keep juglone-sensitive species out of the mature root zone.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun as a pollen source among a hazelnut planting; site it so its bloom overlaps female cultivars such as Lewis or Clark, but pair Jefferson plantings with a different pollenizer such as Gamma.

directions: Delta (OSU 510.041) is one of four Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant pollenizer hazelnuts Oregon State University released together in January 2002, bred to carry the disease-resistance gene originally identified in the old Pacific Northwest cultivar Gasaway. Rather than being grown for its own nut crop, Delta exists to shed pollen that overlaps the bloom window of midseason through very late-flowering female cultivars like Lewis and Clark, filling gaps left as blight resistance breeding retired older pollenizers. Because Delta shares an incompatibility allele with Jefferson, it cannot pollinate Jefferson plantings the way its 2002 sibling release Gamma can, so growers with Jefferson as a main cropping variety need a different pollenizer for that cultivar. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil alongside the female cultivars it is meant to pollinate, treating it as an orchard component rather than a standalone dessert-nut tree.
sources: Oregon State University Extension Service (EM8836, EM9028)
HortScience (Mehlenbacher and Smith, hazelnut pollenizer releases)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun as a very-late pollen source for female cultivars such as Lewis or Clark; do not rely on it to pollinate Jefferson, since their flowering alleles clash.

directions: Epsilon (OSU 669.073) is another of the four Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant pollenizer hazelnuts Oregon State University released in January 2002, developed to keep pollen available for the new generation of blight-resistant female cultivars after older pollen sources were retired. Its pollen is shed very late in the season, which overlaps well with late-flowering cultivars like Lewis and Clark, but because it shares an incompatibility allele with Jefferson, it cannot be used to pollinate Jefferson plantings and growers need a different pollenizer there. As with the other 2002 OSU pollenizer releases, it carries the Gasaway-derived blight resistance gene and is planted purely as a pollen source rather than for its own nut crop. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil within the orchard, positioned to overlap bloom with the compatible female cultivars it is meant to serve.
sources: Oregon State University Extension Service (EM8836, EM9028)
HortScience (Mehlenbacher and Smith, hazelnut pollenizer releases)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun as a very-late pollen source for female cultivars such as Lewis or Clark; it is not a suitable pollenizer for Jefferson due to incompatible flowering alleles.

directions: Zeta (OSU 670.095) completes the set of four Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant pollenizer hazelnuts Oregon State University released in January 2002 alongside Gamma, Delta, and Epsilon, all bred to carry the Gasaway-derived blight resistance gene while supplying pollen for the program's new resistant female cultivars. Like Epsilon, its pollen sheds very late in the season and overlaps well with late-blooming cultivars such as Lewis and Clark, but it shares an incompatibility allele with Jefferson and so cannot serve as its pollen source. Growers plant it purely as an orchard pollen supplier rather than for its own nut harvest, choosing it specifically to extend pollen availability late into the hazelnut bloom period. Site it in full sun on well-drained soil near the compatible female cultivars it is intended to pollinate.
sources: Oregon State University Extension Service (EM8836, EM9028)
HortScience (Mehlenbacher and Smith, hazelnut pollenizer releases)
